text: EX-99.1 2 eh260853599_ex9901.htm EXHIBIT 99.1 EXHIBIT 99.1 Transcript: Brad Jacobs Conference Call Operator: Before we begin, the comments today will include forward-looking statements . Forward-looking statements are not guaranteed, and actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied in forward-looking statements. The comments will also refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures. The company has provided reconciliations of these non-GAAP financial measures to GAAP measures in its press release, which is available on the company’s website. I’ll now turn the call over to Brad Jacobs. Brad Jacobs: Good morning! With me today in Greenwich are QXO’s Chief Strategy Officer, Matt Fassler, and Chief Investment Officer, Mark Manduca. The purpose of this call is twofold. First, I’ll cover the new venture I’m starting, as announced earlier today. And then, we’ll spend most of the time on the excellent progress we’re making at QXO. This includes our pre-released third quarter results, our detailed progress with core components of the business, and the opportunities ahead. After our prepared remarks, Matt, Mark, and I will be happy to take your questions. To launch the new venture, I’ll be leading a $1 billion cash investment in what will be the ninth company I’ve started. As described in today’s press release, my family office, Jacobs Private Equity, together with a group of minority co-investors, has agreed to invest in a public company called CKX Lands. CKX is listed on the NYSE American under the ticker CKX. The investment is expected to consist of $900 million from me and $100 million from co-investors led by Heritage Partners, formerly Sequoia Heritage. Upon closing, I’ll own a majority stake in CKX and become its chairman and CEO, while continuing to serve as chairman and CEO of QXO. CKX is currently a land management company. It earns its revenue from royalty interests and mineral leases related to oil and gas production on its land, as well as timber sales and surface rents. The industry for my new venture is still to be determined. Once we close the investment, CKX will become a platform for growth, operating as a standalone public company under a new name. The proposed transaction is intended to give CKX’s existing stockholders the opportunity to receive an upfront cash payment of $20.8 million, retain the value of the existing business, and participate in the potential upside of our future plans. Completion of the investment remains subject to applicable closing conditions, including CKX stockholder approval. 1 of 28 Over my career, I’ve founded and led eight billion-dollar or multibillion-dollar businesses, including six public companies. I love building multibillion-dollar market leaders, and I’m excited to have the opportunity to do it again. My approach to creating value has been consistent across a wide range of industries—bring in exceptional people, improve operations, invest in technology, and grow both organically and through disciplined acquisitions. My teams and I have completed approximately 500 M&A transactions across these businesses. Last year, I concluded my chairmanships of XPO, GXO, and RXO. That gave me the capacity to create this new venture, while continuing to lead QXO to its massive potential. So now, let’s talk about QXO. I want to emphasize that I remain intensely committed to QXO. My enthusiasm for this company is sky high, and the progress we’re making gives me even more confidence in our ability to accelerate organic growth, expand margins, and create substantial shareholder value. As you may have gathered from our preliminary release this morning, the month of September came in much stronger than expected. We pre-released third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $557 million, on revenue of $4.9 billion, and with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 11.4%. We’ll provide many more details later this week in our earnings release and 10-Q, but suffice it to say, the quarter ended on a high note. Today, I want to focus on why we’re so excited about the progress we’re making at QXO and the positive outlook from here. Our acquisitions of Beacon, Kodiak, and TopBuild gave us leadership positions in some of the most important parts of the building products industry, extensive customer relationships, and management depth. These are the critical attributes to create substantial shareholder value. In North America, we’re now the number one distributor of insulation products, number one in waterproofing, number two in roofing, and number one or number two in lumber and building materials in key regions. We’re also the number one installer in the insulation space. Our company’s 28,000 employees serve 194,000 customers through a network of 1,150 branches across all 50 states and seven Canadian provinces. Our customers include residential, commercial, and industrial general contractors, subcontractors of all types including roofing, insulation, and framing, as well as production and custom homebuilders. Our third-quarter performance demonstrates that our strategy is working across the board. We’re achieving stronger pricing, customer engagement, cross-selling, and service execution. These are accelerating sales trends and profitable market share gains. 2 of 28 Companywide, in the third quarter, trends in organic revenue per day improved for the second consecutive quarter. And pricing improved overall by 2.2% year-over-year, with 9 of our 11 areas delivering positive pricing. In Roofing and Waterproofing, sales of higher-margin complementary products grew 4.2% to $607 million, including 16% growth in gutters and accessories, 15% in fiber cement, and 7% in windows. Private-label penetration in Roofing and Waterproofing also reached a record 10.6% of sales, up about 50 basis points year-over-year. Together, these results demonstrate our growing ability to capture a greater share of customer spending across a broader range of products. Sales momentum accelerated into October, with daily sales increasing 5.4% year-over-year across the company by month’s end. Roofing and Waterproofing, which we have owned the longest, grew 9.1% in October. These results build on a year of profitable market share gains and demonstrate the growing impact of our commercial initiatives and service improvements. In the third quarter, on-time delivery in Roofing and Waterproofing improved by 650 basis points, and out-of-stocks for key products improved more than 25%. Invoice accuracy improved from the low 90s at the outset of the year to the high 90s in the third quarter. Face-to-face customer meetings increased 57% from July to early November. A third of our regions are already exceeding our 95% on-time delivery target, with a large opportunity to replicate these improvements across the network. Critically, our commercial momentum is translating into improved profitability. In Q3, year-over-year gross margin in Roofing and Waterproofing inflected positively from the prior year, despite the soft external environment. We’re encouraged by the direction of the metrics, and we’re still in the early stages of realizing the benefits of the changes underway. Our Insulation distribution business continues to perform well, with revenue accelerating in Q3. We generated a particularly strong performance in our mechanical insulation distribution unit, which posted a strong 16% year-over-year revenue increase, due in part to its leading position with data centers. Our pricing to customers is a major, company-specific lever for us. Importantly, our investments in growth have strengthened our ability to earn more price by improving the customer experience and creating a more compelling value proposition. We’ve built a broader offering, wider product availability, and faster customer service, with more reliable deliveries. We’ve instilled more rigorous governance over excessive price overrides and improved the tools, management, and 3 of 28 incentives that support pricing decisions. Our goal is to price consistently, based on data, and in a way that’s fair to our customers and to QXO. Companywide, our year-over-year pricing has improved by 400 basis points, from negative 1.7% in April to positive 2.3% in September. Pricing turned positive in June and has strengthened in each subsequent month throughout Q3. Roofing and Waterproofing showed an even larger improvement over the same period, moving from negative 1.1% in April to positive 4.1% in September. These metrics demonstrate our ability to improve pricing even during the current soft environment. Going forward, we’re implementing sophisticated pricing analytics across the acquired businesses, and we see multiple runways to improve pricing, including the commercial deal process, customer-specific price negotiations, and linking quoting decisions more closely to customer profitability. Procurement is another major lever for us. We’ve established centralized category leadership, and we’re in the process of bringing our spend together across the businesses. Our three major acquisitions have approximately $12 billion of spend, including about $11 billion in direct products and materials, and more than $1.1 billion in indirect goods and services. Approximately $7.6 billion of that spend is with suppliers serving at least two of legacy Beacon, Kodiak, or TopBuild. This includes over 1,000 direct suppliers and about 200 indirect suppliers. Within that overlap, approximately $5 billion is with suppliers serving all three legacy businesses. These existing supplier relationships represent an opportunity to align pricing, rebates, and contract terms, and to negotiate using our combined purchasing power. We’re pursuing these opportunities through coordinated negotiations, supplier consolidations, stronger rebate capture, and wider adoption of common purchasing agreements. Our goal is to reward strategic supplier partners with more of our business, allowing them to grow rapidly with us, while we improve cost, availability, and service for our customers. We’ve already realized procurement synergies across a number of indirect categories, such as fleet, technology, and waste disposal. Cross-selling is another key focus as we continue to integrate the three businesses. We have about 194,000 unique customers, and almost none of them currently buy our full product offering. We already have ongoing relationships with these customers, and in many cases, we’re already on their job sites. We’ve developed a good sense of their requirements and their total spend. Our goal is to earn a much larger share of their business and drive substantial organic 4 of 28 growth. The majority of our customers have compelling reasons to consolidate suppliers and reduce complexity. Many need multiple categories of traditional building materials, and some also need engineered components. The total scope of our offering can help customers reduce their total construction cost, address labor shortages, simplify procurement, and mitigate project delays. For example, our strong relationships with production homebuilders are typically rooted in our truss and wall panel capabilities, as well as insulation where we solve some of their greatest needs. At the same time, it creates an opportunity for us to expand share of wallet by becoming their primary supplier for a wider range of building materials, with the added value of scale to support their growth. We’re achieving early success with a cross-selling pilot in Tampa where we serve 18 trades. The pilot is surfacing the time and cost efficiencies QXO can bring to a single project by combining distribution, installation services, and field management across the trades. By coordinating crews and services, we can eliminate duplicate trips to job sites, reduce material handling, improve scheduling, and shorten construction cycles. For example, we can combine interior trim and garage door installation into a single visit or arrange to have the work performed on site. We can also help customers realize scalable savings in their most precious resource— labor—including time spent in coordination and construction. These same benefits apply to large-scale commercial projects like data centers. In some geographies, we can supply foundation rebar, insulation, roofing, waterproofing, and commercial doors for the same project, creating a unique value proposition for customers. That contractor has fewer supplier relationships to manage, with meaningful time and cost benefits, and we earn a greater share of the business. We can extend that opportunity even further with project-level visibility. For example, our technology will tell us whether we’ve supplied a hospital’s roofing, mechanical insulation, building insulation, doors, and other requirements, allowing us to pursue the categories we’re missing. Now, we’re also making a concerted effort to reactivate dormant accounts. Between the companies we bought, there are tens of thousands of dormant customers, including 2,000 substantial ones who, together, used to do nearly half a billion dollars of business with our legacy companies. We want that business back. Private label is another attractive part of the business. Our TRI-BUILT brand now represents 10.6% of our Roofing and Waterproofing sales, which is an all-time high. The gross 5 of 28 margin on private label is substantially higher than on similar, market-branded products. We’re developing additional TRI-BUILT categories and giving our salespeople incentives to sell private label. Trailing 12-month TRI-BUILT sales at the end of Q3 were $943 million, all of it at legacy Beacon. Our target is to grow this to more than $2 billion over the next three years, while also expanding private label at legacy Kodiak and TopBuild operations. In terms of execution, we’re putting experienced operators into branches that are underperforming their potential and introducing common operating metrics to identify opportunities for greater efficiency. We’re focusing on four fundamentals: frequent customer contact, disciplined pricing, appropriate staffing, and agile inventory management. Legacy TopBuild used this approach effectively in its lower-performing locations, and we’re extending it across the company, demonstrating a key benefit of quality M&A: applying proven operating practices where they can have the greatest impact. We’re even more excited today about TopBuild than we were when we announced the acquisition. Bringing TopBuild into QXO has given us additional commercial exposure, including major, multi-year projects, and a presence at approximately 22,000 job sites every day. We have substantial opportunities to deepen these customer relationships, cross-sell products and services, and capture a greater share of wallet. On the installation side, we have highly experienced installers who know how to complete a job efficiently and pass inspection. We can build on that expertise by strengthening sales management, improving training for new hires, and giving employees better technology. Technology will help us accelerate many of the improvements. I’m extremely pleased with the tech team we’ve assembled and the tech roadmap we’re executing. We’re implementing a new ERP system, a proprietary point-of-sale system, an upgraded CRM platform with advanced AI capabilities, and a warehouse management system. We’re also integrating tools for pricing and procurement, fleet technology, e-commerce, and human resources. When this is fully rolled out, our employees will be able to get their work done in one connected, AI-enabled environment. They’ll be able to spend less time entering the same information into different systems or tracking down information that will be readily available. The new ecosystem will give our people more capacity to serve customers and run the business. We’re currently testing the tech in a number of locations under real-life operating conditions and training employees to use it. Then, we’ll accelerate the rollout. 6 of 28 Our expectation is to have the vast majority of revenue across legacy TopBuild, Beacon, and Kodiak on the new platform over the next year. This will deliver significant advantages by making transactions easier to complete and, improving the overall customer experience. We’ll be able to create quotes in seconds or minutes rather than hours or days, provide real-time visibility into inventory and order status, and automate inventory scanning, slotting, and picking. More efficient inventory replenishment will reduce working capital requirements without compromising customer fulfillment. And we’ll use the tools to optimize logistics, with more efficient loads and routes equating to a reduction in transportation costs. In addition, we’re improving our e-commerce capabilities so customers can check inventory, get accurate quotes, place orders, and track deliveries online. The goal is to make it easy for customers to do business with QXO, so that each time they use us, we earn their loyalty for the next transaction. AI is a key driver of both operational excellence and margin expansion. One project we’re particularly encouraged by could effectively double sales force productivity in one of our business units. More broadly, we see the potential to boost productivity in a number of daily workflows. Let me put all of these opportunities in the context of our long-term plan. Our goal is to grow adjusted EBITDA from the approximately $1.75 billion reflected in current consensus estimates to $4 billion by 2030, before additional acquisitions. This takes into account market growth, share gains, productivity improvements, and synergies as we integrate Kodiak and TopBuild. In addition, we believe there will continue to be opportunities to purchase small businesses on highly accretive terms. Between now and 2030, we estimate that acquisitions we can fund with internally generated cash flow could contribute up to $1.5 billion of additional EBITDA, taking the total EBITDA opportunity to approximately $5.5 billion by 2030. Our operations are highly cash-generative, and we have no debt maturities prior to 2031. We have a covenant-lite capital structure and over $2 billion of available liquidity. Nearly two-thirds of our debt stack is fixed rate. We have substantial flexibility to invest in organic growth and pursue accretive acquisitions. The operating metrics are inflecting upward, and we’re still in the early stages of realizing benefits from the strong foundation we’ve built. We have a large, highly satisfied customer base, served by experienced operators. We have a big opportunity to make the business more productive and much more valuable over time. So, to sum up, there’s a lot of excitement in the room. There’s a new 7 of 28 venture on the horizon. We feel great about QXO’s performance and outlook. And we look forward to meeting you face-to-face at key forums in the coming days and weeks. I remain wholeheartedly committed to QXO, and I’m confident in our ability to execute the plan we’ve outlined this morning. Thank you for your interest and your support. We’ll now open the call for questions. Operator? Operator: Thank you. We'll now be conducting a question and answer session. We ask you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. If you'd like to ask a question at this time, you may press star one on your telephone keypad and a confirmation tone will indicate your lines in the question queue. You may press star two if you like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Thank you. And our first question is from the line of Trevor Allinson with Wolfe Research. Please proceed with your questions. Trevor Allinson: Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. You guys have been clearly very busy over the last 12 to 18 months with acquisitions, technology, implementation among other things. If you could in your own words, summarize, you know, everything that you've done, all the changes you guys have implemented at QXO over the last year, year and a half. Thanks. Brad Jacobs: Well, that would be a long answer, but I'll try my best. Uh, what have we accomplished in the last year and a half? Uh, in a word or maybe two words. A lot. A real lot. Uh, first, we started by concentrating on the people. We have 28,000 team members. And we wanted to make sure that every single one of those 28,000 people understands the vision of what we intend to accomplish here. That we're creating a world-class building products distributor and installer. And we will be recognized by customers as the leading provider of these products and services. And we made sure that everybody knows what the vision is and what their role is in accomplishing that vision. And we started to tie compensation to how well people delivered on their levers. And we upgraded talent where necessary. We improved the org chart. We reduced unnecessary layers in the org chart. We rightsized spans of control, and we invested in the development of our people. Specifically, for 8 of 28 example, we created what we call Precision Leadership Training, which is a proprietary course in how to be an effective leader of people and it's gotten rave reviews from our managers who are both early in career and late in career and we're expanding this training to our sales organization now. I, by the way, I was delighted that Forbes recently named us one of the 20 most trusted companies in America. I think that's pretty cool for a company that's only been around for a year or two. And it's not it's not coincidental. We we've mobilized the entire company to focus on the key levers. And let's go over those key levers. I'll try to be brief. So, on sales, one important thing we've done is we've redesigned compensation incentives so that we're rewarding salespeople on what we want them to focus on, like cross-selling, for example, and we we're rewarding people for selling private label. Our private label margin is about 2,000 basis points higher than the rest of our product mix. So, that's a high priority for us. We reactivated 3,300 dormant accounts, and we've got tens of thousands of dormant account opportunities to go. We've increased face-to-face customer meetings. We've introduced data-driven pricing. We've largely centralized procurement and strengthened strategic relationships with our key suppliers. We've intensely focused on operational excellence. We've optimized the inventory mix. We've optimized on-time and in-full. We've optimized invoice accuracy. So, everything that goes into excellently running the business. And we designed a cutting-edge tech stack that, once we fully implement it, will definitely differentiate us in the eyes of the customer and will also give us a big cost advantage in terms of productivity and efficiency. So, let me point out the main components of the tech stack. We have a next gen point of sales system that we've designed. We've got a warehouse management system, a transportation management system. We got pricing tools. We have an AI-enabled CRM. We got procurement bots, and all these things are connected on a unified, modern ERP and we've already rolled out dozens, maybe hundreds, but many, many bespoke productivity and efficiency tools uh e-commerce so we believe that e-commerce is going to be more and more in more and more important channel over the next decade for our customers. That's what we're hearing from customers: they want to save time. E-commerce helps them save time. So, we've developed an omnichannel platform that integrates all the customer touch points, e-commerce, physical branches, sales reps, mobile apps, everything related to the to customer service and put it into one seamless 9 of 28 shopping experience that'll save customers time, that'll lower our cost to serve them, and ultimately should increase our share of customer spend. And I think the proof is in the pudding. When you look at the numbers and do the work, you see the results. For example, we're obviously in a very weak external market, but companywide pricing is up 2.2%. And look at the trend in the pricing. So, go back to April. In April, pricing was down 1.7% year-over-year. In May it was also down, but not as much. Down only 0.5%. And then, pricing inflected positive in June. June it was up 1.1%. And July was up a little bit more, 1.2%. August was up a little bit more than that, 1.8%. And in September, it was up 2.3%. Look at roofing. In roofing, the improvement in pricing was even more pronounced. April was down 1.1%. May was flat. June was up 1.9%. July was up 2.9%. August was up 3.6%. And September was up 4.1%. So, a really nice trend there, with year-over-year margin trends inflecting positively in Q3. Starting in the fourth quarter, October companywide daily sales increased 5.4% year-over-year. So nice trend here. And in roofing, which we've owned the longest, daily sales were up in October 9.1%. So, look, customers are very demanding, and they should be. They want a lot of things from us and the thing they want the most is product availability. They want us to have in stock what they want to buy when they want to buy it. They want us to say yes pretty much all the time. So, we categorize all of our inventory as either A, B, or C depending on the turns, the velocity, the turns, how fast moving each SKU is. And on A items where, we want to be in-stock almost all the time, we've improved the out-of-stocks by more than 25%. On-time and in-full delivery, another very important thing for our customers, year-over-year you look at OTIF, on-time and in-full, it's up 650 basis points, a really good improvement there. Invoice accuracy, another really important thing for customers, was in the low 90s, now in the high 90s. Uh face-to-face customer meetings, getting in front of customers, finding out what they need, bonding with them, helping them solve their problems. Face-to-face customer meetings up 57% since July. Uh, I talked about private label in the opening remarks. Very important for us because it's 2,000 basis points higher than the rest of our mix. We're now up to 10.6% of our of our roofing sales. So, really good progress there. So, the bottom line for me is: we've addressed virtually every part of the company, from people, to sales, to pricing, to procurement, ops, tech. I'm sure I'm leaving one or two things out. Pretty much everything in the company and we've made tremendous progress in a very short period of 10 of 28 time. And we're just beginning to realize the benefits of all these activities. So, sorry the long speech, but I get very excited about this stuff. Thanks for the question, Trevor. Operator: The next question is from the line of Garik Shmois with DA Davidson. Please proceed with your question. Garik Shmois: Oh, hi. Thanks for taking my question. I was hoping you could expand on how you get from the $1.75 billion of EBITDA to $4 billion by 2030. And if you can just give us some updated building blocks uh in the bridge, that would be great. Thanks. Brad Jacobs: Uh yes, I can. Uh, both I’ll give you the how we get there, I give you the building blocks block. So, thanks for the question, Gary. Uh it's a very clear roadmap to get from where we are now, roughly $1.75 billion of EBITDA to $4 billion by 2030. And by the way, the $4 billion of EBITDA 2030 assumes we just take all the free cash flow that we expect to generate between now and 2030 and just take that and pay down debt with it. If instead we took that free cash flow and did small acquisitions at single digit EBITDA multiples, that gets us to $5.5 billion in EBITDA. So, the main levers to answer your question are the mainly the things I've been talking about: sales, pricing, procurement, inventory management, operational excellence, and all that underpinned by state-of-the-art technology and a and a very highly motivated workforce and let me give you a little detail on almost all those. So, start with sales. So, we now have 194,000 customers, general contractors, subcontractors of all different types, home builders of all sizes, from the big production guys to regional and custom builders. And those customers are spread across the whole spectrum: residential, commercial, industrial, including data centers. And as I said in the prepared remarks, uh we don't we don't have a lot of cross-selling going on today—yet. We will. We have a fantastic relationships with those 194,000 customers, but we're typically selling them only a small part of what we could support them because we bought three different companies. They weren't those three companies were independent when we bought the models. So, take a data center for example. We may have a fantastic relationship, and we have we do have fantastic relationship with lots and lots of data centers, but we're mainly selling an installation, and there's no reason 11 of 28 why we can't also be selling them waterproofing, for example. Every data center needs waterproof. There's no reason we can't be selling them roofing. They all need roofs. Uh data centers don't need a lot of windows, but we can sell them a lot of doors. So, the cross-selling opportunity, not just with data centers, but throughout those customers we got, it's really enormous. And there's no, in my mind, no better customer to get more business from than a customer you're already serving. So cross-selling is a big, big, big part of our future. Homebuilders, home builders are a big opportunity, too. One of the main reasons we bought Kodiak is that they brought phenomenal relationships with the big production home builders and the custom builders. And they were mainly selling them lumber or truss trusses or engineered products. So, we're building on those great relationships and we're going to sell them much much more. And we've already started talking to many of these customers about this. There's a lot of appetite for this. I talked about dormant accounts a few minutes ago. So, these are customers already have an account open with us. We know them, they know us. No matter why they left, we want to get their business back. And that's a that's another big opportunity. Another lever is private label. I talked about that earlier, too. We make 2,000 basis points higher margin on private label than the rest business. So, we're motivating our sales force to sell more private labels and we're going to add more SKUs under our private label. Pricing. Pricing is a, maybe I should start with pricing because it’s such a huge lever. We've made a lot of progress on pricing, but man, we've got a long way to go. The goal is to have pricing done objectively based on data using algorithms that take into account price elasticity and have everything integrated across the system. Meaning the order fill rates, the amount of time that customer, the percentage of time a customer asks uh for a quote and we're able to say yes, we have that in stock. Here's our here's our quote. Uh demand forecasting, inventory management, and pricing is intimately intertwined with all those things and you need the tech to process all that information in real time and deliver what's the right price. It's fair for us and fair for fair for the customer. So pricing is your best lever in pretty much any business because there's just no cost associated with it, so any extra price goes right to pre-tax. And I'm not just talking about raising prices, it's optimizing prices. I think we're on a good trajectory to getting price where it needs to be, and I think we have an excellent pricing team. I'm very optimistic about continuing that momentum. So, a lot of data, a 12 of 28 lot of data crunching and tech enablement. Procurement. As a distributor, we're a distributor and an installer, but as a distributor, procurement is very very important. As we get bigger and grow, we will deserve and earn better rebates, and we will pass some of those savings from the rebates on to our customers, and we'll keep some of that for ourselves. Let's talk about indirect procurement. Indirect procurement, we have thousands of suppliers. I'm talking about everything from rent and garbage removal to pens and papers and computers to toilet paper. And we've made very good progress on this. And now that we've owned all three companies for a few months. We have a huge opportunity to unify all of our spend. So, you don't have one branch buying Pepsi and another branch buying Coke, and or you have one branch buying office supplies from Staples, another branch buying from Office Depot. I mean there's nothing really visionary about this. We we've done this many many times at several companies over the years, and it's fairly mathematical and the outcome is predictable. You consolidate suppliers, get a lot of savings, particularly as we get, and that that's those savings increase as we earn it as we get bigger. Let's talk about direct procurement. So, direct procurement what do we want? We want deep relationships with a smaller number of strategic supplier partners. We want to be important partners with them and preferably their most important partner. And there's quite a lot of overlap among the key suppliers across the three acquisitions we've recently done. We have a number of suppliers who we now buy over a billion dollars a year from, and many many more that we buy hundreds of millions of dollars from. So, we want to get the billion-dollar price or the hundreds of millions of dollars price, and that's only fair. Let's talk about inventory management. We're investing so we have the right products in the right place at the right time. And availability of our fast-moving A items is has been going up. We still have ways to go, but we've gone up a lot lot lot, and we've significantly reduced out-of-stocks on those on those A items. So, we're able to say yes much much more often than predecessor companies were able to. Look, anybody can lower price to win lower margin or unprofitable market share. We're not doing that. We're in investing in a better customer experience and getting inventory right is a real big part of that. And that's how we earn the right to take share and get a little more price by giving customers better value. That's very core to what we're doing here. It's laser focused on the customer experience, with all the things I I've been talking about, and therefore the 13 of 28 customers want to do more business with us and they're willing to pay a little bit more because the value is better. Another lever is the underperforming branches. So, most of our branches are doing very well, but like any company, particularly one that's just completed three significant acquisitions, we have a minority that are a significant minority that that are underperforming. Now, ironically, I consider that a good thing in the sense that we could turn those underperforming branches into better-performing branches and that's a kind, that's a contributor to the roadmap. All the things that we're working on, all the levers They're supported by technology innovation, and we need leading-edge tech to do all these things. And if we want customers to make us their first call or their first place that they go, we need to have a system that helps them get in and out fast, gets them accurate information right away, and facilitates being on-time and in-full in terms of last mile delivery, and great technology enables all that. And there's a big variance between companies that can hit the hit the ball out of the park on all these components and those that can't. Technology is the is the enabler in my opinion. By the way, the technology also gives us a cost advantage because we can run the business more intelligently, more efficiently, more knowledgeably. And the last lever I would list would be people. Maybe I should have said that first because people are so critical to the whole the whole plan. But, we're constantly refining the org chart and the compensation so that we can motivate and reward fairly people for doing the right things, for helping customers and fulfilling our mission to be the most customer-centric company in this industry, and I want QXO to be a powerful magnet for talent. So, I want this to be the company that everyone in the industry wants to come work for and ultimately I want that to be reflected in the stock market by the highest multiple in the industry.
